title: New research finds AI adoption is associated with more managers—and different managerial skills
excerpt: A Strategic Management Journal study challenges the assumption that AI adoption automatically reduces demand for managers. Liudmila Alekseeva, José Azar, Mireia Giné and Sampsa Samila analyze U.S. job postings from 2010 to 2022, linking firm-level AI adoption with managerial vacancies and skill requirements.
content_html:
A Strategic Management Journal study challenges the assumption that AI adoption automatically reduces demand for managers. Liudmila Alekseeva, José Azar, Mireia Giné and Sampsa Samila analyze U.S. job postings from 2010 to 2022, linking firm-level AI adoption with managerial vacancies and skill requirements.

In instrumental-variable estimates, a 1-percentage-point increase in AI-related job-posting share is associated with a 1.2-percentage-point increase in managerial share—about 7.5%—and roughly a 9% increase in managerial vacancies.

The relationship is strongest in manufacturing and among R&D-intensive firms. Managerial skill demand also changes. AI-intensive firms place less emphasis on routine administrative capabilities such as budgeting and planning and more on stakeholder management, creativity, sales management and other growth-oriented skills.

The authors do not interpret the estimates as definitive causal effects, and the study primarily covers predictive AI rather than the newer generative and agentic systems. For leaders, the implication is to redesign management rather than assume automation simply removes managers. AI can reduce routine tasks while increasing the need for coordination, scaling and organizational adaptation.

Publication details

Liudmila Alekseeva et al., Artificial intelligence adoption and the demand for managerial expertise, Strategic Management Journal (2026). DOI: 10.1002/smj.70099
